title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: Ferndean Manor was a building of considerable age, moderate size, and no architectural ambition, buried deep in a wood. I had heard of it before. Mr. Rochester often spoke of it and sometimes visited. His father had bought the estate for its hunting grounds. He would have rented the house but could find no tenant, because of its remote and unhealthy location. So Ferndean remained empty and unfurnished, except for two or three rooms fitted up for the squire's use when he went there in shooting season.

I reached this house just before dark on an evening marked by grey skies, a cold wind, and steady, penetrating rain. The last mile I walked, having dismissed the carriage and driver with the double payment I'd promised. Even when I was very close to the manor, I could see nothing of it—so thick and dark were the trees of the gloomy wood around it. Iron gates between granite pillars showed me where to enter. Passing through them, I found myself at once in the twilight of close-ranked trees. A grass-grown track led down the forest aisle between gnarled, moss-grown trunks and under arching branches. I followed it, expecting soon to reach the house, but it stretched on and on, winding farther and farther, with no sign of any dwelling or grounds.

I thought I had taken a wrong turn and lost my way. The darkness of nature and forest gathered around me. I looked for another path. There was none—only interwoven branches, thick trunks, and dense summer foliage. Not an opening anywhere.

I kept going. At last the trees thinned a little. Soon I made out a railing, then the house—barely distinguishable from the trees in the dim light, so damp and green were its decaying walls. I entered through a door fastened only with a latch and stood in an enclosed yard from which the wood curved away in a half circle. There were no flowers, no garden beds—only a broad gravel walk circling a patch of grass, set in the heavy frame of the forest. The house presented two pointed gables in its front. The windows were latticed and narrow. The front door was narrow too—one step led up to it. The whole looked, as the innkeeper had said, "quite a desolate spot." It was as still as a church on a weekday—the only sound anywhere around was the rain pattering on the forest leaves.
"Can there be life here?" I asked.
Yes—life of some kind was there. I heard a movement. That narrow front door was opening, and some shape was about to emerge.

It opened slowly. A figure came out into the twilight and stood on the step—a man without a hat. He stretched out his hand as if to feel whether it was raining. Dusk as it was, I had recognized him—it was my master, Edward Fairfax Rochester, and no other.

I stayed where I was, almost holding my breath, and stood to watch him—to study him, myself unseen, and, alas, invisible to him. It was a sudden meeting, one in which joy was kept firmly in check by pain. I had no trouble holding back my voice from crying out, or my step from rushing forward.

His form was the same strong, powerful build as ever. His bearing was still upright. His hair was still raven-black. His features were still sharp and firm—not in one year's time could any sorrow have worn down his athletic strength or blighted his prime. But in his face I saw a change—a look of desperate brooding that reminded me of some wronged and chained wild animal or bird, dangerous to approach in its sullen misery. A caged eagle, its gold-ringed eyes put out by cruelty, might have looked as that blind Samson looked.

And, reader, do you think I feared him in his blind fury? If you do, you don't know me. A gentle hope blended with my sorrow that soon I would dare to press a kiss on that rocky brow, and on those lips so sternly sealed beneath it—but not yet. I would not approach him yet.

He stepped down from the doorstep and moved slowly, gropingly, toward the grass. Where was his bold stride now? Then he stopped, as if unsure which way to turn. He raised his hand and opened his eyes—gazing blankly, straining toward the sky and the ring of trees around him: you could see that to him it was all empty darkness. He stretched out his right hand (he kept the left, the maimed one, hidden in his coat), as if trying to feel his way to some sense of what lay around him—but he met only air, for the trees stood some yards off from where he was. He gave up the attempt, folded his arms, and stood quiet and silent in the rain, now falling fast on his bare head. At this moment John came toward him from somewhere nearby.
"Will you take my arm, sir?" said a voice. It was John. "There's a heavy shower coming on. You'd better go in."
"Leave me alone," was the answer.
John withdrew without noticing me. Mr. Rochester tried again to walk about—in vain. Everything was too uncertain. He groped his way back to the house and re-entered it. I heard him close the door.
I now approached and knocked. John's wife opened for me. "Mary," I said, "how are you?"

She started as if she had seen a ghost. I calmed her. To her flustered "Is it really you, miss, come at this late hour to this lonely place?" I answered by taking her hand. Then I followed her into the kitchen, where John now sat by a good fire. I explained in a few words that I had heard everything that had happened since I left Thornfield, and that I had come to see Mr. Rochester. I asked John to go down to the turnpike house, where I had left the chaise, and bring back my trunk. Then, while I took off my bonnet and shawl, I asked Mary whether I could be put up at the Manor House for the night, and finding that it could be managed, though not easily, I told her I would stay. Just then the parlour bell rang.
"When you go in," I said, "tell your master that a person wishes to speak to him, but don't give my name."
"I don't think he'll see you," she answered. "He refuses everybody."
When she returned, I asked what he had said.
"You are to send in your name and your business," she replied. She then proceeded to fill a glass with water and place it, with candles, on a tray.
"Is that what he rang for?" I asked.
"Yes. He always has candles brought in at dark, even though he's blind."
"Give the tray to me. I will carry it in."
I took it from her hand. She pointed me toward the parlour door. The tray shook as I held it. The water sloshed from the glass. My heart pounded. Mary opened the door for me and shut it behind me.

The parlour looked grim. A neglected handful of fire burned low in the grate. Leaning over it, with his head supported against the tall, old-fashioned mantelpiece, stood the blind tenant of the room. His old dog, Pilot, lay on one side, curled up as if afraid of being accidentally stepped on. Pilot pricked his ears when I came in. Then he jumped up with a yelp and bounded toward me. He almost knocked the tray from my hands. I set it on the table, then patted him and said softly, "Lie down!" Mr. Rochester turned mechanically to see what the commotion was, but since he saw nothing, he turned back and sighed.
"Give me the water, Mary," he said.
I approached him with the now only half-filled glass. Pilot followed me, still excited.
"What is the matter?" he asked.
"Down, Pilot!" I said again. He paused with the glass halfway to his lips, and seemed to listen. He drank, and put the glass down. "This is you, Mary, is it not?"
"Mary is in the kitchen," I answered.

He put out his hand quickly, but not seeing where I stood, he didn't touch me. "Who is this? Who is this?" he demanded, seeming to try to see with those sightless eyes—a useless, distressing effort! "Answer me—speak again!" he ordered, loud and commanding.
"Will you have a little more water, sir? I spilled half of what was in the glass," I said.
"Who is it? What is it? Who speaks?"
"Pilot knows me, and John and Mary know I am here. I came only this evening," I answered.
"Great God!—what delusion has come over me? What sweet madness has seized me?"
"No delusion—no madness. Your mind, sir, is too strong for delusion, your health too sound for madness."
"And where is the speaker? Is it only a voice? Oh! I cannot see, but I must feel, or my heart will stop and my brain will burst. Whatever you are—whoever you are—let me touch you, or I cannot live!"
He groped. I caught his wandering hand and held it in both of mine.
"Her very fingers!" he cried. "Her small, slight fingers! If so, there must be more of her."
The strong hand broke free from mine. My arm was seized, my shoulder—neck—waist—I was pulled close and gathered to him.
"Is it Jane? What is it? This is her shape—this is her size—"
"And this her voice," I added. "She is all here—her heart, too. God bless you, sir! I am glad to be so near you again."
"Jane Eyre!—Jane Eyre," was all he said.
"My dear master," I answered, "I am Jane Eyre. I have found you out—I have come back to you."
"In truth? In the flesh? My living Jane?"
"You touch me, sir. You hold me, and tightly enough. I am not cold like a corpse, nor empty like air, am I?"

"My living darling! These are certainly her limbs, and these her features. But I cannot be so blessed, after all my misery. It is a dream—such dreams I have had at night when I clasped her once more to my heart, just as I do now. And kissed her, as thus—and felt that she loved me, and trusted she would not leave me."
"Which I never will, sir, from this day on."

"Never will, says the vision? But I always woke and found it an empty mockery. And I was desolate and abandoned—my life dark and lonely—my soul thirsting and forbidden to drink—my heart starved and never fed. Gentle, soft dream, nestled in my arms now, you will fly too, as all your sisters fled before you—but kiss me before you go. Embrace me, Jane."
"There, sir—and there!"

I pressed my lips to his once-brilliant, now sightless eyes. I swept the hair from his brow and kissed that too. He suddenly seemed to rouse himself: the conviction that all this was real took hold of him.
"It is you—is it, Jane? You have come back to me, then?"
"I have."
"And you do not lie dead in some ditch? And you are not a starving outcast among strangers?"
"No, sir! I am an independent woman now."
"Independent! What do you mean, Jane?"
"My uncle in Madeira is dead, and he left me five thousand pounds."

"Ah! That is practical—that is real!" he cried. "I should never dream that. Besides, there is that particular voice of hers—so lively and sharp, as well as soft. It revives my withered heart; it puts life into it. What, Janet! Are you an independent woman? A rich woman?"
"Quite rich, sir. If you won't let me live with you, I can build a house of my own close to your door, and you may come and sit in my parlour whenever you want company in the evening."
"But as you're rich, Jane, you must now have friends who will look after you and not let you devote yourself to a blind man like me?"
"I told you I am independent, sir, as well as rich. I am my own mistress."
"And you will stay with me?"

"Certainly—unless you object. I will be your neighbor, your nurse, your housekeeper. I find you lonely. I will be your companion—to read to you, to walk with you, to sit with you, to wait on you, to be eyes and hands to you. Stop looking so gloomy, my dear master. You will not be left desolate, so long as I live."

He didn't answer. He seemed serious—withdrawn. He sighed. He half-opened his lips as if to speak, then closed them again. I felt a little embarrassed. Perhaps I had leapt over the proprieties too rashly, and he, like St. John, saw impropriety in my forwardness. I had made my offer, in truth, because I believed he wished—and would ask—me to be his wife: an expectation, unspoken but no less certain for that, had kept my spirits up, that he would claim me for his own at once. But no hint of that escaped him, and his face grew more clouded, and I suddenly remembered I might be entirely wrong, and was perhaps unwittingly making a fool of myself. I began gently to draw back from his arms—but he caught me and pulled me close again.

"No—no—Jane; you must not go. No—I have touched you, heard you, felt the comfort of your presence—the sweetness of your consolation. I cannot give up these joys. I have little left in myself—I must have you. The world may laugh—may call me absurd, selfish—no matter. My very soul demands you. It will be satisfied, or it will take deadly vengeance on its frame."
"Well, sir, I will stay with you. I have said so."

"Yes—but you understand one thing by staying with me, and I understand another. You, perhaps, could bring yourself to be about my hand and chair—to wait on me like a kind little nurse, since you have an affectionate heart and a generous spirit that lead you to make sacrifices for people you pity—and that, no doubt, ought to be enough for me. I suppose I should now feel nothing but fatherly affection for you: do you think so? Come—tell me."
"I will think whatever you like, sir. I am content to be only your nurse, if you think it better."
"But you cannot always be my nurse, Janet. You are young—you must marry one day."
"I don't care about being married."
"You should care, Janet. If I were what I once was, I would try to make you care—but—a sightless block!"

He fell back into gloom. I, on the contrary, grew more cheerful and took fresh courage. These last words showed me where the trouble lay, and since it was no trouble to me at all, I felt entirely free of my earlier embarrassment. I went on in a livelier vein of conversation.

"It's time someone undertook to bring you back to human shape," I said, parting his thick, long, uncut hair. "I see you're being turned into a lion, or something of the sort. You've got a distinct look of Nebuchadnezzar out in the fields about you, that's certain—your hair reminds me of eagle feathers. Whether your nails have grown like bird claws, I haven't yet checked."
"On this arm, I have neither hand nor nails," he said, drawing the mutilated limb from his chest and showing it to me. "It is a mere stump—a ghastly sight! Don't you think so, Jane?"
"It is a pity to see it. And a pity to see your eyes—and the scar of fire on your forehead. And the worst of it is, one is in danger of loving you too much for all this and making too much of you."
"I thought you would be revolted, Jane, when you saw my arm and my scarred face."

"Did you? Don't tell me that—or I might say something unflattering about your judgment. Now, let me leave you for a moment to make a better fire and have the hearth swept up. Can you tell when there's a good fire?"
"Yes—with the right eye I see a glow—a reddish haze."
"And you see the candles?"
"Very dimly—each is a glowing cloud."
"Can you see me?"
"No, my fairy. But I am grateful enough to hear and feel you."
"When do you have supper?"
"I never have supper."
"But you shall have some tonight. I am hungry—so are you, I expect. Only you've forgotten it."

I called for Mary and soon had the room in better order. I prepared him a comfortable meal, too. My spirits were high, and I talked to him with ease and pleasure all through supper, and for a long while after. There was no strain between us, no holding back my liveliness for his sake—with him I was completely at ease, because I knew I suited him; everything I said or did seemed to comfort him or bring him back to life. It was a wonderful thing to feel. It woke my whole nature into light: in his presence I truly lived, and he lived in mine. Blind as he was, smiles crossed his face, joy rose on his forehead; his features softened and warmed.

After supper, he began to ask me many questions—where I had been, what I had been doing, how I had found him. But I gave him only partial answers; it was too late that night to go into particulars. Besides, I didn't want to touch any deep, aching chord, or open some fresh well of feeling in his heart—my only aim for now was to cheer him. And cheered he was, as I've said, though only in fits and starts. If a moment's silence broke the conversation, he would grow restless, touch me, and say, "Jane."
"You are altogether a human being, Jane? You are certain of that?"
"I truly believe so, Mr. Rochester."

"Yet how, on this dark and gloomy evening, could you so suddenly appear at my lonely hearth? I reached out my hand to take a glass of water from a servant, and it was given me by you. I asked a question, expecting Mary's voice to answer—and your voice spoke to my ear."
"Because I had come in, in Mary's place, with the tray."

"And there's enchantment in this very hour I'm spending with you. Who can say what a dark, bleak, hopeless life I've dragged through these past months? Doing nothing, expecting nothing, letting night blur into day—feeling only the cold when I let the fire go out, the hunger when I forgot to eat. And beneath it all, a ceaseless sorrow, and at times a sheer delirium of longing to see my Jane again. Yes—I longed for her return far more than I ever longed for my lost sight. How can it be that Jane is with me, and says she loves me? Won't she vanish as suddenly as she came? Tomorrow, I'm afraid, I'll find her gone."

A plain, practical reply, cutting against the current of his troubled thoughts, was, I was sure, the best comfort I could offer. I ran my finger over his eyebrows and remarked that they were scorched, and that I would put something on them to make them grow back as thick and black as ever.

"What's the use of doing me good in any way, kind spirit, when at some fatal moment you'll desert me again—passing away like a shadow, gone I don't know where or how, and afterward impossible for me to find?"
"Have you a pocket comb about you, sir?"
"What for, Jane?"
"Just to comb out this shaggy black mane. I find you rather alarming at close range. You talk of my being a fairy, but I'm sure you look more like a brownie yourself."
"Am I hideous, Jane?"
"Very, sir. You always were, you know."
"Hmph! The mischief hasn't been taken out of you, wherever you've been."
"Yet I have been with good people—far better than you. A hundred times better. People with ideas and views you never entertained in your life. Much more refined, and with much better manners."
"Who on earth have you been with?"
"If you twist around like that, you'll make me pull the hair out of your head. And then I think you'll stop suspecting I'm a phantom."
"Who have you been with, Jane?"

"You won't get it out of me tonight, sir. You must wait until tomorrow. Leaving my tale half-told will, you know, be a kind of guarantee that I'll show up at your breakfast table to finish it. And I must remember not to appear at your hearth with only a glass of water next time—I'll have to bring at least an egg, not to mention fried ham."

"You mocking creature—fairy-born and human-raised! You make me feel as I haven't felt in twelve months. If Saul could have had you for his David, the evil spirit would have been exorcised without the need for a harp."
"There, sir—you're tidied up and made presentable. Now I'll leave you. I have been traveling for three days, and I believe I'm tired. Goodnight."
"Just one word, Jane: were there only ladies in the house where you've been?"
I laughed and made my escape, still laughing as I ran upstairs. "A good idea!" I thought with glee. "I see I have the means of teasing him out of his melancholy for some time to come."

Very early the next morning I heard him up and moving about, wandering from one room to another. As soon as Mary came down, I heard the question: "Is Miss Eyre here?" Then: "Which room did you put her in? Is she up? Go and ask if she wants anything. And when she'll come down."

I came down as soon as I thought breakfast might be ready. I entered the room very softly and had a view of him before he noticed I was there. It was mournful, really, to see that vigorous spirit subdued by physical helplessness. He sat in his chair—still, but not at rest, clearly waiting for something; the lines of a now-habitual sadness marked his strong features. His face reminded me of a lamp put out, waiting to be relit—and, sadly, it was no longer within his own power to kindle that light of animated expression: he depended on someone else for that now. I had meant to be cheerful and easy, but the sight of that strong man made powerless touched me to the quick. Still, I greeted him with what liveliness I could manage.
"It is a bright, sunny morning, sir," I said. "The rain is over and gone, and there's a soft glow after it. You'll have a walk soon."
I had wakened the glow: his features lit up.

"Oh, you really are there, my skylark! Come to me. You're not gone—not vanished? I heard one of your kind an hour ago, singing high over the wood, but its song had no music for me, any more than the rising sun had light. All the melody on earth is gathered in my Jane's voice to my ear—and I'm glad it's not naturally a silent one. All the sunshine I can feel is in her presence."

Tears stood in my eyes to hear him admit his dependence like this—just as if a royal eagle, chained to a perch, had been forced to beg a sparrow to become its provider. But I would not give in to tears. I wiped them away and busied myself with preparing breakfast.

Most of the morning was spent outdoors. I led him out of the wet, wild wood into some cheerful fields. I described to him how brilliantly green they were, how refreshed the flowers and hedges looked, how sparkling blue the sky was. I found him a seat in a hidden, lovely spot—a dry tree stump—and didn't refuse, once he was seated, to let him pull me onto his knee. Why should I, when we were both happier close than apart? Pilot lay beside us; everything was quiet. He broke out suddenly, holding me in his arms—

"Cruel, cruel deserter! Oh, Jane, what did I feel when I discovered you had fled from Thornfield, and could find you nowhere—when I searched your room and found you'd taken no money, nor anything that could serve in its place! A pearl necklace I'd given you lay untouched in its little box; your trunks were left corded and locked, just as they'd been packed for the wedding trip. What was my darling to do, I wondered, left destitute and penniless? And what did she do? Let me hear it now."

Prompted by his urgency, I began the story of my experience over the past year. I softened considerably what related to the three days of wandering and starvation, because to tell him everything would have caused him needless pain—the little I did say wounded his faithful heart more deeply than I wished.

He said I shouldn't have left him that way, with no means of making my way in the world. I should have told him my intention. I should have confided in him—he would never have forced me to become his mistress. Violent as he'd seemed in his despair, he in truth loved me far too well and too tenderly to make himself my tyrant. He would have given me half his fortune, without asking so much as a kiss in return, rather than let me throw myself, friendless, on the wide world. He was certain I had suffered more than I'd admitted to him.

"Well, whatever my sufferings had been, they were very short," I answered. And then I told him how I had been taken in at Moor House. How I had obtained the position of schoolmistress. The inheritance and the discovery of my relatives followed in due order. Of course, St. John Rivers' name came up frequently. When I had finished, that name was immediately seized upon.
"This St. John, then, is your cousin?"
"Yes."
"You've spoken of him often. Do you like him?"
"He was a very good man, sir. I couldn't help liking him."
"A good man. Does that mean a respectable, well-behaved man of fifty? Or what does it mean?"
"St. John was only twenty-nine, sir."
"Still young, then. Is he a short, dull, plain man? The kind whose goodness lies more in the absence of vice than in any real strength of character?"
"He is tirelessly active. Great and noble deeds are what he lives for."
"But his mind? Probably rather soft? He means well, but you'd shrug listening to him talk?"
"He speaks very little, sir. What he does say is always to the point. His mind is first-rate—not easily swayed, but powerful."
"Is he an able man, then?"
"Truly able."
"A thoroughly educated man?"
"St. John is an accomplished and profound scholar."
"His manners, I think, you said aren't to your taste? Stuffy and preachy?"
"I never mentioned his manners. But unless I have very bad taste, they must suit me. They are polished, calm, and gentlemanly."
"His appearance—I forget how you described it. Some sort of raw young curate, half-strangled by his white collar and tottering on thick-soled boots?"
"St. John dresses well. He is a handsome man—tall, fair, with blue eyes and a Grecian profile."
"Damn him!" (Aside.) Then to me: "Did you like him, Jane?"
"Yes, Mr. Rochester, I liked him. But you asked me that before."

I could see what he was doing, of course. Jealousy had seized him. It stung—but the sting was healthy. It gave him a break from the gnawing fang of melancholy. So I didn't immediately soothe the snake.
"Perhaps you'd rather not sit on my knee any longer, Miss Eyre?" came the next, somewhat unexpected remark.
"Why not, Mr. Rochester?"

"The picture you've just painted suggests a rather overwhelming contrast. Your words have sketched a graceful Apollo—tall, fair, blue-eyed, with a Grecian profile. Your eyes rest on a Vulcan—a real blacksmith, brown, broad-shouldered, and blind and lame into the bargain."
"I never thought of it before, but you certainly do resemble Vulcan, sir."
"Well, you may leave me, ma'am. But before you go"—and he held me with a firmer grip than ever—"just answer me a question or two." He paused.
"What questions, Mr. Rochester?"
Then followed this cross-examination.
"St. John made you schoolmistress of Morton before he knew you were his cousin?"
"Yes."
"You would often see him? He'd visit the school sometimes?"
"Daily."
"He would approve of your plans, Jane? I know they'd be clever, because you are a talented creature!"
"He approved of them—yes."
"He would discover many things in you he hadn't expected? Some of your accomplishments aren't ordinary."
"I don't know about that."
"You had a little cottage near the school, you say. Did he ever come there to see you?"
"Now and then."
"In the evenings?"
"Once or twice."
A pause.
"How long did you live with him and his sisters after the family connection was discovered?"
"Five months."
"Did Rivers spend much time with the women of his family?"
"Yes. The back parlour was both his study and ours. He sat near the window, and we sat by the table."
"Did he study a lot?"
"A good deal."
"What?"
"Hindustani."
"And what did you do in the meantime?"
"I studied German, at first."
"Did he teach you?"
"He didn't know German."
"Did he teach you nothing?"
"A little Hindustani."
"Rivers taught you Hindustani?"
"Yes, sir."
"And his sisters too?"
"No."
"Only you?"
"Only me."
"Did you ask to learn?"
"No."
"He wanted to teach you?"
"Yes."
A second pause.
"Why did he want to? What use could Hindustani be to you?"
"He intended me to go with him to India."
"Ah! Now we reach the heart of the matter. He wanted you to marry him."
"He asked me to marry him."
"That's a lie—an outrageous invention to torment me."
"I beg your pardon, it's the plain truth. He asked me more than once, and was just as stubborn about pressing his case as you ever were."
"Miss Eyre, I repeat, you may leave me. How often must I say the same thing? Why do you remain planted on my knee when I've told you to go?"
"Because I'm comfortable here."

"No, Jane, you are not comfortable—because your heart isn't with me. It's with this cousin—this St. John. Oh, until this moment I thought my little Jane was all mine! I believed she loved me even when she left me. That was a drop of sweetness in the bitterness. For all the time we've been apart, for all the hot tears I've wept over our separation, I never imagined that while I was mourning her, she was loving another! But it's no use grieving. Jane, leave me—go and marry Rivers."
"Shake me off, then, sir—push me away. I won't leave on my own."
"Jane, I've always loved your voice. It still gives me hope—it sounds so true. When I hear it, it carries me back a year. I forget that you've formed a new attachment. But I'm not a fool—go—"
"Where must I go, sir?"
"Your own way—with the husband you've chosen."
"Who is that?"
"You know—this St. John Rivers."

"He is not my husband, and never will be. He doesn't love me. I don't love him. He loves—as much as he can love, which is not the way you love—a beautiful young woman called Rosamond. He wanted to marry me only because he thought I'd make a suitable missionary's wife, which she would not. He is good and great, but severe. And for me, cold as an iceberg. He is not like you, sir. I am not happy at his side, nor near him, nor with him. He has no indulgence for me—no fondness. He sees nothing attractive in me; not even youth—just a few useful qualities of mind. Then must I leave you, sir, to go to him?"
I shuddered involuntarily, and pressed closer to my blind but beloved master. He smiled.
"What, Jane! Is this true? Is this really how things stand between you and Rivers?"

"Absolutely, sir! Oh, you have no reason to be jealous! I wanted to tease you a little, to make you less sad. I thought anger would be better than grief. But if you want me to love you, could you but see how much I do, you would be proud and satisfied. My whole heart is yours, sir. It belongs to you. And with you it would stay, even if fate exiled the rest of me from your presence forever."
Again, as he kissed me, painful thoughts darkened his face.
"My ruined sight! My crippled strength!" he murmured with regret.

I stroked his face to soothe him. I knew what he was thinking and wanted to speak for him, but didn't dare. As he turned away for a moment, I saw a tear slide from under the sealed eyelid and trickle down his cheek. My heart swelled.

"I am no better than the old lightning-struck chestnut tree in Thornfield orchard," he said after a while. "And what right would that ruin have to ask a flowering vine to cover its decay with fresh green?"

"You are no ruin, sir—no lightning-struck tree. You are green and full of life. Plants will grow around your roots whether you ask them to or not, because they delight in your generous shade. And as they grow, they'll lean toward you and wind around you, because your strength offers them the safest support."
Again he smiled. I was giving him comfort.
"You speak of friends, Jane?" he asked.
"Yes, of friends," I answered, somewhat hesitantly. I knew I meant more than friends but couldn't find another word. He helped me.
"Ah! Jane. But I want a wife."
"Do you, sir?"
"Yes. Is that news to you?"
"Of course. You said nothing about it before."
"Is it unwelcome news?"
"That depends on circumstances, sir—on your choice."
"Which you shall make for me, Jane. I'll accept your decision."
"Choose then, sir—her who loves you best."
"I will at least choose—her I love best. Jane, will you marry me?"
"Yes, sir."
"A poor blind man, whom you'll have to lead by the hand?"
"Yes, sir."
"A crippled man, twenty years older than you, whom you'll have to wait on?"
"Yes, sir."
"Truly, Jane?"
"Most truly, sir."
"Oh! My darling! God bless you and reward you!"

"Mr. Rochester, if I ever did a good deed in my life—if I ever thought a good thought—if I ever prayed a sincere and blameless prayer—if I ever wished a righteous wish—I am rewarded now. To be your wife is, for me, to be as happy as I can be on earth."
"Because you delight in sacrifice."

"Sacrifice! What do I sacrifice? Famine for food. Waiting for fulfillment. To be allowed to put my arms around what I treasure—to press my lips to what I love—to rest against what I trust: is that a sacrifice? If so, then yes—I delight in sacrifice."
"And to put up with my weaknesses, Jane. To overlook my flaws."
"Which are nothing to me, sir. I love you better now, when I can truly be useful to you, than I did when you were proud and independent—when you'd accept no role but that of the giver and protector."

"Until now I've hated being helped—being led. From now on, I think I shall hate it no more. I didn't like putting my hand into a hired servant's. But it's a pleasure to feel Jane's little fingers around it. I preferred total loneliness to the constant presence of servants. But Jane's quiet care will be a perpetual joy. Jane suits me. Do I suit her?"
"To the very core of my being, sir."
"Then we have nothing in the world to wait for. We must be married at once."
He looked and spoke with eagerness. His old fire was rising.
"We must be joined without delay, Jane. There's only the license to get—then we marry."
"Mr. Rochester, I've just noticed the sun is well past noon, and Pilot has actually gone home for his dinner. Let me look at your watch."
"Fasten it to your belt, Janet, and keep it. I have no use for it."
"It's nearly four in the afternoon, sir. Aren't you hungry?"
"The third day from now must be our wedding day, Jane. Never mind fine clothes and jewels—none of that matters."
"The sun has dried up all the rain, sir. The breeze is still. It's quite warm."
"Do you know, Jane, I have your little pearl necklace around my neck at this moment, tucked under my collar? I've worn it since the day I lost my only treasure—as a reminder of her."
"We'll go home through the wood. That will be the shadiest way."
He pursued his own thoughts without heeding me.

"Jane! You think me, I'm sure, a godless man. But my heart swells with gratitude to the merciful God of this earth right now. He sees not as man sees, but far more clearly. He judges not as man judges, but far more wisely. I did wrong. I would have stained my innocent flower—breathed guilt on its purity. The Almighty snatched it from me. I, in my stubborn rebellion, nearly cursed the punishment. Instead of bowing to the decree, I defied it. Divine justice followed its course. Disasters came thick upon me. I was forced to pass through the valley of the shadow of death. His punishments are mighty, and one struck me that has humbled me forever. You know I was proud of my strength—but what is it now, when I must hand it over to someone else's guidance, like a child does its weakness? Only lately, Jane—only lately—I began to see and acknowledge the hand of God in my fate. I began to feel remorse, repentance, the wish to be reconciled with my Maker. I began sometimes to pray—very brief prayers, but very sincere.

"Some days ago—four days, to be exact—last Monday night, a strange mood came over me. Grief replaced frenzy. Sorrow replaced bitterness. I had long been convinced that since I couldn't find you anywhere, you must be dead. Late that night—perhaps between eleven and midnight—before going to my miserable bed, I begged God, if it pleased Him, to take me soon from this life and admit me to the next world, where there was still hope of reunion with Jane."

"I was in my room, sitting by the open window. The mild night air soothed me. I could see no stars—only by a faint, luminous haze did I know the moon was out. I longed for you, Janet! Oh, I longed for you with soul and flesh! I asked God, in anguish and humility, whether I had not been desolate and tormented long enough. Whether I might not soon taste peace and happiness again. I admitted I deserved everything I'd endured—but I pleaded that I could scarcely bear any more. And the sum of my heart's whole desire broke involuntarily from my lips in the words: 'Jane! Jane! Jane!'"
"Did you speak those words aloud?"
"I did, Jane. If anyone had heard me, they'd have thought me insane. I said them with such desperate force."
"And it was last Monday night, near midnight?"

"Yes. But the time doesn't matter. What followed is the strange part. You'll think me superstitious—there's some superstition in my blood, and always has been. But this is true—at least it is true that I heard what I'm about to tell you.

"As I cried 'Jane! Jane! Jane!' a voice—I cannot tell where it came from, but I know whose voice it was—replied, 'I am coming: wait for me.' And a moment later, the wind carried a whisper: 'Where are you?'

"Let me try to tell you, if I can, the idea, the picture those words opened in my mind—though it's hard to put into words. Ferndean is buried, as you see, in heavy woodland, where sound falls flat and dies without echo. 'Where are you?' seemed to be spoken among mountains, for I heard a hill-sent echo repeat the words. At that moment the wind seemed to grow cooler and fresher on my brow. I could have believed that, in some wild, lonely place, Jane and I were meeting. In spirit, I believe we must have met. You no doubt were, at that hour, asleep and unaware, Jane—perhaps your soul wandered from its body to comfort mine. Because that was your voice—as sure as I'm alive—it was yours!"

Reader, it was on Monday night—near midnight—that I too had received the mysterious call. Those were the very words with which I had answered it. I listened to Mr. Rochester's account but said nothing in return. The coincidence struck me as too strange and awe-inspiring to discuss. If I told anything, my story would inevitably make a deep impression on his mind—and that mind, already too prone to dark thoughts from suffering, did not need the added weight of supernatural mystery. I kept these things in my heart.

"You can't wonder, then," my master continued, "that when you appeared before me so unexpectedly last night, I had difficulty believing you were anything more than a voice and a vision—something that would dissolve into silence, as the midnight whisper and mountain echo had dissolved before. Now, I thank God! I know otherwise. Yes, I thank God!"

He set me down from his knee, rose, and reverently lifted his hat from his head. Bending his sightless eyes toward the earth, he stood in silent devotion. Only the last words of his prayer were audible.
"I thank my Maker that, in the midst of judgment, He has remembered mercy. I humbly beg my Redeemer to give me strength to lead a purer life than I have lived until now!"

Then he reached out his hand to be led. I took that dear hand, held it a moment to my lips, then let it rest around my shoulder. Being so much shorter than he, I served as both his support and his guide. We entered the wood and made our way home.
